offers.title: You've won a bike!
offers.story: A text says: 'Well done! You have won a brand-new bike! Just pay $25 for delivery today to get it.' But you never entered any competition.

options.text: Text back: 'Is this real?'
options.result: 'Yes, 100% real!' they replied. Of course they did. Now they know your number works, and more silly texts arrive.
options.lesson: Never reply to a scam text. Just delete it.

options.text: Pay the $25: a new bike is worth way more
options.result: No bike ever came. The $25 went to a scammer, and now they keep texting you for more.
options.lesson: If you have to pay to get a prize, it isn't a prize.

options.text: Delete it: you can't win something you never entered
options.result: Smart! The same text went to thousands of phones. It was a scam, and your $25 stays safe in your pocket.
options.lesson: You can't win a competition you never entered.

options.text: Show it to a grown-up you trust
options.result: Your mum took one look: 'That's a scam!' She showed you how to block the number.
options.lesson: If a message feels odd, show someone you trust before you do anything.

offers.title: Football shirts for $3
offers.story: A stranger opens a big bag at your stall. 'Shirts of the city's top football team! Only $3 each. Cash only, no receipt.' In the club shop, the same shirt costs $50.

options.text: Ask him for a receipt first
options.result: 'No receipts!' he said, and hurried away. That told you everything you needed to know.
options.lesson: An honest seller is always happy to give you a receipt.

options.text: Ask him if the shirts are real
options.result: 'Of course they're real!' he grinned. You believed him and bought five. In the wash, every badge peeled off.
options.lesson: Anyone can say 'it's real'. Believe proof, not promises.

options.text: Buy 10 and sell them at your stall for $20 each
options.result: The shirts were fakes, and the badges peeled off in the wash. Customers wanted their money back, and some stopped coming.
options.lesson: A famous brand at a tiny price is a fake, and selling fakes is against the law.

options.text: Say 'No thanks': too cheap and no receipt means trouble
options.result: He shrugged and walked off. Later you heard his shirts were fakes. Phew! Your money stayed safe.
options.lesson: Super cheap, cash only and no receipt? Walk away.

offers.title: A jar for the puppies
offers.story: A man shakes a jam jar with a paper label: 'Save the Puppies!' 'Please give me all the money you made today, $40,' he says. 'Quick, I have to go!'

options.text: Say 'Not today' and carry on selling
options.result: You kept your money. But he went on to trick the stall next door, because nobody warned anyone.
options.lesson: Spotting a trick is great. Warning others is even better.

options.text: Ask to see his badge, then check the charity's name
options.result: He had no badge and hurried off. Real collectors carry a badge, use a sealed tin and never rush you.
options.lesson: Real charities are happy for you to check. Tricksters rush you.

options.text: Give him the $40: the puppies need help!
options.result: There was no puppy charity. The money went into his own pocket, and not one puppy got any help.
options.lesson: Tricksters look for kind hearts. Check a charity before you give.

options.text: Tell the market manager about him
options.result: The manager knows every real collector. This man wasn't one, so he was asked to leave the market.
options.lesson: If something feels wrong, tell a grown-up who is in charge.

offers.title: A call from 'the bank'
offers.story: Your phone rings. 'Hello, this is your bank! Someone is trying to take your money. We just sent you a code by text. Read it to me now, quickly, so we can stop them!'

options.text: Hang up, then ring the bank on the number on your card
options.result: The real bank said: 'We would never ask for your code!' Your money was safe all along.
options.lesson: Hang up and call back on a number you already know.

options.text: Ask the caller to prove they really are the bank
options.result: They knew your name and sounded very kind. Scammers can do that too! You hung up, but only just in time.
options.lesson: A scammer can know your name and sound friendly. Check another way.

options.text: Hand the phone to a grown-up
options.result: Your dad listened, said 'No, thank you' and hung up. 'Banks never ask for codes,' he said.
options.lesson: When a call rushes you, hand it to someone you trust.

options.text: Read out the code fast to save your money
options.result: The caller wasn't the bank. The code let them into your account, and they took money before you could stop them.
options.lesson: Never share a code someone texts you, even with 'the bank'.

offers.title: A stall at the summer fair
offers.from: a poster at the town hall
offers.story: The town's summer fair wants stalls. The poster says: 'Book a stall for $30 on the council website.' Outside, a man whispers: 'Give me $60 cash and I'll get you the best spot!'

options.text: Book on the council website, just as the poster says
options.result: The fair was packed! Your stall was busy all day, and you made a great profit, even after the $30.
options.lesson: Check it's official, then go for it. Good chances are real too.

options.text: Pay the man $60 for the best spot
options.result: He had no spots to sell. On the day, your name wasn't on the list, and the $60 was gone.
options.lesson: Never pay a stranger for something you can book yourself.

options.text: Don't go: big events are always a trick
options.result: The fair was real and great fun. The other stalls made lots of money, but you missed it.
options.lesson: Not every offer is a trick. Check it, then decide.

options.text: Share a stall with a friend and split the $30
options.result: Half the cost and half the space. You had a fun day, and you both made a little profit.
options.lesson: Sharing a cost is a smart way to try something new.

offers.title: New bank details?
offers.story: An email that looks just like your main supplier's says: 'We have changed banks. Please pay this month's bill of $2,400 into our new account today, or your deliveries will stop.'

options.text: Pay the new account today so deliveries don't stop
options.result: The email came from a scammer copying your supplier. The $2,400 is gone, and you still owe the real bill.
options.lesson: An email can look exactly like a company's and still be fake.

options.text: Phone the supplier on the number you've always used
options.result: 'We never sent that!' said the supplier. You saved $2,400, and they warned all their other customers.
options.lesson: Changed bank details? Check by phoning a number you already know.

options.text: Pay the old account as usual and delete the email
options.result: Your money went to the right place. But nobody warned the supplier, so two other shops got tricked.
options.lesson: Spotted a scam? Tell the company it copied, so it can warn others.

options.text: Ring the phone number written in the email to check
options.result: A friendly voice said, 'Yes, it's us!' But it was the scammer's phone. You paid, and the $2,400 vanished.
options.lesson: Never check a message using a number or link inside that message.

offers.title: 500 five-star reviews
offers.from: a message from a marketing company
offers.story: A company messages you: 'Get 500 five-star reviews for your shops for just $300! Real-looking names, all posted this week. Everybody does it!'

options.text: Reply kindly to every review, good or bad
options.result: Customers loved that you listened. One grumpy reviewer even changed their two stars to four!
options.lesson: Answering reviews kindly shows customers you care.

options.text: Buy the 500 reviews: more stars, more customers
options.result: The review website spotted the fakes, deleted them and put a warning on your page. Customers stopped trusting you.
options.lesson: Fake reviews are cheating, and they get found out.

options.text: Ask happy customers to leave an honest review
options.result: A little card by the till did it. Forty real reviews came in, and new customers believed every one.
options.lesson: A few real reviews beat hundreds of fake ones.

options.text: Get your staff and family to write five-star reviews
options.result: The website noticed the reviews all came from the same few people and removed them. A bit embarrassing!
options.lesson: Reviews must come from real customers, not your friends and family.

offers.title: Join the Golden Circle
offers.story: Your old friend Jake messages: 'Join the Golden Circle! Pay $1,000, then find 3 friends who pay $1,000 each. When they each find 3 more, you get $8,000!' What does it sell? 'Nothing,' says Jake. 'People just join!'

options.text: Join quickly, before everyone else does
options.result: Your 3 friends joined, but their friends didn't. The circle stopped, its boss vanished, and you all lost your $1,000.
options.lesson: If the money only comes from new people joining, most people lose.

options.text: Say no, and gently tell Jake you're worried for him
options.result: Jake was cross at first. But he got out before he lost more, and later he thanked you.
options.lesson: A real friend tells you the truth, even when it's awkward.

options.text: Join, and sign up your staff to get your money back
options.result: The circle soon stopped. Your staff lost $1,000 each and felt let down by you, and two of them left.
options.lesson: Never pull people who trust you into a get-rich scheme.

options.text: Do the maths: who pays when people stop joining?
options.result: 3 people, then 9, 27, 81... By round 21 it would need more people than live on Earth! You kindly said no.
options.lesson: Do the maths on any 'get rich' plan. If it needs endless new people, it fails.

offers.title: A grant from the council
offers.from: a letter from the city council
offers.story: The council writes: shops can get a $5,000 grant (money you never pay back) for energy-saving lights and fridges. Apply free on the council website. Next day a man rings: 'I'll do the forms for you. My fee is $800, paid now.'

options.text: Check the council's website, then apply yourself
options.result: The grant was real, and the form took twenty minutes. New lights went in, and your power bills went down.
options.lesson: Real grants are free to apply for. Find them on the official website.

options.text: Bin the letter: free money is always a scam
options.result: The grant was real. The shop next door got new lights and lower bills, and you missed out.
options.lesson: Some free help is real. Check the official website before you say no.

options.text: Pay the man $800 so you can skip the forms
options.result: He wasn't from the council at all. He took the $800 and never filled in a single form.
options.lesson: Never pay a stranger to get you money that is free.

options.text: Ask other shop owners if they have applied
options.result: Two had, and said it was real! But by the time you applied, most of the money was gone, so your grant was smaller.
options.lesson: Asking people you know is a good check, but don't wait too long.

offers.title: A wholesaler's deal
offers.from: a sales rep from Harbour Foods
offers.story: Mei from Harbour Foods, a wholesaler (it sells to shops in bulk), offers 15% off flour, milk and fruit for a one-year deal. She leaves the contract and a list of shops she supplies. That evening a stranger rings: 'I'll do 40% off if you pay for the whole year today!'

options.text: Say no to both: salespeople always trick you
options.result: Harbour Foods was honest. The bakery down the road signed, and now it sells cheaper bread than you.
options.lesson: Saying no to everything means missing the good deals too.

options.text: Sign Mei's deal on the spot: 15% off is too good to miss
options.result: The deal was real, but you missed page 3: you must buy $3,000 of food every month. Lots of it went to waste.
options.lesson: Read every page before you sign, even when the deal is real.

options.text: Ring two shops on her list, read the contract, then sign
options.result: Both shops loved Harbour Foods, and the contract was fair. Your food cost less all year.
options.lesson: Check references and read the contract. Then a good deal is safe to take.

options.text: Take the stranger's 40% off and pay for the year today
options.result: One delivery came, then nothing. The stranger's phone stopped working, and a whole year's money was gone.
options.lesson: A much cheaper deal that wants all the money first is a big warning sign.

offers.title: Half-price office
offers.from: an advert on a property website
offers.story: Your team needs a bigger office. An advert shows a smart Downtown office at half the usual rent. The 'agent' says: 'Three companies want it! Pay a $20,000 deposit today to hold it. I'm abroad, so you can only see it next month.'

options.text: Look up the building's owner in the official records
options.result: The records (a public list of who owns each building) showed a different owner. She said it wasn't for rent. Scam spotted!
options.lesson: Check who really owns a building before you pay anything.

options.text: Insist on seeing it first, with the owner or a known agent
options.result: The 'agent' stopped answering at once. A local agent you trust then found you a real office at a fair rent.
options.lesson: See it, meet the real owner, then pay. A real deal will wait for a visit.

options.text: Pay the deposit now, before another company gets it
options.result: The photos were copied from a real office that was never for rent. The 'agent' vanished with your $20,000.
options.lesson: Never pay for a place you haven't seen, and never because someone rushes you.

options.text: Pay half now and the rest once you've seen it
options.result: Half was still $10,000 lost. There was no office to see, and the 'agent' never answered again.
options.lesson: Paying a scammer a little is still losing money.

offers.title: Urgent: log in today!
offers.from: an email to all your staff
offers.story: All 40 of your staff get an email from 'IT Support': 'Your email closes today! Log in at this link to keep it.' The link looks like your company's website, but one letter is different. Two staff have already typed in their passwords.

options.text: Phone your real IT team and ask them to block the link
options.result: 'Not from us!' said the IT team, and blocked the link. But nobody changed the two passwords until the next day: a close call.
options.lesson: Check with the real team, on a number you know.

options.text: Tell everyone to log in quickly so no email closes
options.result: The link was a fake page that collected passwords. Hackers read your emails and tricked a customer into paying them.
options.lesson: Never type a password into a link from an email. Go to the website yourself.

options.text: Ignore it: it's only an email
options.result: The two passwords let hackers in. They sent fake bills to your customers, and fixing it cost money.
options.lesson: When someone clicks a bad link, act straight away. Waiting makes it worse.

options.text: Warn everyone, change the two passwords, add two-step login
options.result: Fast work! The passwords were changed in time, and two-step login (a code on your phone, like a second lock) kept hackers out.
options.lesson: Act fast on a fake email: warn everyone, change passwords, add a second lock.

offers.title: A 'fast-track fee'
offers.from: a man from the planning office
offers.story: You want to make one of your buildings bigger. Planning permission (the council's OK to build) usually takes six months. A man from the planning office says: 'Pay me a $15,000 fast-track fee in cash, and you'll have it next week. No receipt.'

options.text: Say no politely and wait the six months
options.result: You kept your hands clean, and permission came on time. But the man kept asking other people for cash.
options.lesson: Saying no to a bribe is right. Reporting it stops it happening to others.

options.text: Build without permission and sort it out later
options.result: The council stopped the building work halfway. You paid a fine and still had to wait for permission.
options.lesson: Skipping the rules always costs more than waiting for them.

options.text: Say no, report him, and ask the council for an official fast route
options.result: The council thanked you and stopped him. They showed you an official faster route, with a proper receipt. Permission came in two months.
options.lesson: Say no to bribes and report them. Then ask for the official way.

options.text: Pay the fee: six months is far too long to wait
options.result: It was a bribe, and the man was caught. Your permission was cancelled, you were fined, and the news hurt your good name.
options.lesson: A real fee comes with an official receipt. Secret cash for an official is a bribe.

offers.title: A top chef wants to team up
offers.story: Amara Osei, a chef who runs two popular restaurants, wants to open a new one with you. She runs the kitchen, you provide the building, and you share the profit. She gives you the phone numbers of her two past business partners.

options.text: Call her past partners, get a lawyer to read the deal, then sign
options.result: Both partners praised her. Your lawyer fixed one unclear line, and the new restaurant was full every weekend.
options.lesson: Call a partner's past partners. They know what working together is really like.

options.text: Try it first: run a one-month trial restaurant together
options.result: A month of trial dinners showed you work well together. You signed the full deal, just a little later.
options.lesson: A small trial is a smart way to test a big partnership.

options.text: Say no: business partners always fall out
options.result: Amara opened with someone else. Their restaurant became the talk of Downtown, and you watched from outside.
options.lesson: A partner with proven references can help your business grow faster.

options.text: Sign today: she's famous, so it must be safe
options.result: Amara was honest, but the contract had a typing mistake that gave her your building! Fixing it took months of lawyer bills.
options.lesson: Famous doesn't mean checked. Read every contract before you sign.

offers.title: Your files are locked
offers.from: a message on every company screen
offers.story: One morning every screen says: 'We have locked all your files. Pay a ransom (money to get them back) of $3 million, or we delete everything!' This is a cyber attack. Luckily, your IT team made backups (spare copies of every file) last night.

options.text: Unplug every computer from the internet, then wait
options.result: Unplugging stopped the attack spreading: a good first step! But nothing was fixed until you called in experts.
options.lesson: Unplugging is a good first move, but experts must finish the job.

options.text: Don't pay: call cyber experts and the police, restore backups
options.result: The experts shut the hackers out, the police took the case, and last night's backups brought everything back in two days.
options.lesson: Keep backups. If hackers strike, don't pay: call experts and the police.

options.text: Pay quickly: losing every file would be even worse
options.result: You paid, but only half the files came back, and the hackers asked for more. Paying told them you were an easy target.
options.lesson: Don't pay hackers: there is no promise they'll keep their word.

options.text: Keep it secret and try to fix it yourselves
options.result: The hackers were still hiding inside and struck again. When customers learned you'd kept it secret, many left.
options.lesson: Hiding an attack helps the hackers. Get experts, and be honest with customers.

offers.title: Double your money in 30 days
offers.from: an investor on a video call
offers.story: A smiling investor, Rex, shows you MoonCoin, a new crypto coin (money that only exists online). 'Put in $5 million and I guarantee it doubles in 30 days! A famous footballer has bought some. But this offer ends tonight!'

options.text: Put in $5 million before tonight's deadline
options.result: MoonCoin shot up, then crashed to zero when Rex sold all his coins and vanished. The footballer had never even heard of it.
options.lesson: Guaranteed, huge and only tonight? That's a scam, every single time.

options.text: Ask your financial adviser to check Rex and MoonCoin
options.result: Your adviser found Rex on the official warning list of people not allowed to sell investments. An easy no!
options.lesson: Check an investment seller on the official list before you listen.

options.text: Put in just $50,000 to test it first
options.result: Your screen showed huge gains! But when you tried to take your money out, you couldn't. Then the website vanished.
options.lesson: If you can't take your money out, it was never really yours.

options.text: Say no: nobody can promise to double money in a month
options.result: A month later, MoonCoin was worth nothing and Rex had disappeared. Your money was safe, still working in your businesses.
options.lesson: Real investments never promise big, fast, guaranteed gains.

offers.title: A secret tip from a friend
offers.from: a friend who works at a big company
offers.story: Your friend Sam works at Comet Phones. He whispers: 'Tomorrow we announce a huge deal, and our shares (small pieces of the company) will shoot up. Buy lots tonight. Nobody will know!' Trading on secret news like this is called insider trading.

options.text: Wait until the news is public, then decide
options.result: Once everyone knew, buying was fair. The price had already jumped, so you kept your money in your own businesses.
options.lesson: Once news is public, everyone has a fair chance. That's how it should be.

options.text: Buy $3 million of shares tonight: easy money
options.result: The market watchdog (the team that checks share trading) spotted your big buy. Sam lost his job, and you paid a huge fine.
options.lesson: Trading on secret company news is against the law, and it gets found out.

options.text: Say no, and don't pass the tip on to anyone
options.result: Sam realised it was wrong and told no one else. When the news came out, you both had nothing to hide.
options.lesson: Fair trading uses news everyone can see, never secrets.

options.text: Buy just a little, so nobody notices
options.result: The watchdog checks every trade made just before big news, small ones too. You were fined, and it was in the papers.
options.lesson: A small cheat is still a cheat, and it still gets caught.

offers.title: A loan to grow
offers.story: Your bank offers a $10 million loan at 5% interest (the extra you pay each year for borrowing) to open more branches of your best businesses. Then a 'loan broker' (a go-between) rings: 'Pay my $200,000 fee now, and I'll get you 1%!'

options.text: Borrow $40 million instead: bigger is better
options.result: The repayments were huge. When a slow summer came, you had to sell a business to pay the bank.
options.lesson: Only borrow what you can repay in a bad month, not just a good one.

options.text: Read the terms, compare one other bank, check you can repay
options.result: Your bank's deal was fair and clear, and the repayments fitted even a slow month. The new branches grew your profits all year.
options.lesson: Borrowing is smart when the profit beats the interest and you can always repay.

options.text: Never borrow: loans are always a bad idea
options.result: You stayed safe, but a rival borrowed, grew faster and won the city's new bus contract.
options.lesson: Debt is a tool. Smart CEOs borrow carefully when it pays.

options.text: Pay the broker's $200,000 fee for the 1% deal
options.result: The broker took the fee and stopped answering. Luckily, your own bank's fair offer was still there.
options.lesson: Never pay a stranger upfront to get you a loan. That's a classic scam.
